{{short description|American organic chemist}}
{{use mdy dates|date=May 2021}}

'''Patrick Harran''' (born 13 July 1969) is an American organic chemist who has held the D. J. & J. M. Cram Chair in [[Organic chemistry|Organic Chemistry]], an [[endowed chair]] at the [[University of California, Los Angeles]], since 2008. Prior to taking this position he was a professor at the [[University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Microsoft Word - Web CV 20140121.doc |url=http://www.chem.ucla.edu/harran/harran_vitae.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140819090607/http://www.chem.ucla.edu/harran/harran_vitae.pdf |archive-date=19 August 2014 |website=www.chem.ucla.edu}}</ref> Harran was educated at [[Skidmore College]] graduating in 1990. He went on to Yale University, where he was awarded a Ph.D. in 1995.<ref name=":0" />

In 2009, a research assistant in his lab, Sheri Sangji, died from [[burn]] injuries after a chemical fire.<ref name="Haunting LAT">{{cite news |last1=Christensen |first1=Kim |title=Deadly UCLA lab fire leaves haunting questions |url=https://www.latimes.com/local/lanow/la-xpm-2009-mar-01-me-uclaburn1-story.html |access-date=21 May 2021 |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=1 March 2009}}</ref> A [[California Division of Occupational Safety and Health]] report faulted Harran for willfully neglecting safety protocols.<ref name="LAT report faults">{{cite news |last1=Christensen |first1=Kim |title=Report faults professor, UCLA in death of lab assistant |url=https://www.latimes.com/local/la-me-ucla-lab-20120121-story.html |access-date=21 May 2021 |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=2012-01-21}}</ref> He was charged with four felony counts in [[Sheri Sangji case|the first criminal case]] stemming from a [[laboratory accident]] in U.S. history, but avoided jailtime through a [[plea deal]] with prosecutors, which was finalized in 2018.<ref name="Avoids jailtime LAT">{{cite news |last1=Christensen |first1=Kim |title=UCLA chemistry professor avoids prison time in fatal lab fire case |url=https://www.latimes.com/local/lanow/la-me-ln-ucla-professor-avoids-prison-fatal-lab-fire-20140620-story.html |access-date=21 May 2021 |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=2014-06-20}}</ref><ref>url=https://cen.acs.org/safety/lab-safety/Charges-dropped-against-UCLA-chemistry/96/web/2018/09 |access date=23 July 2021</ref>  In 2015, the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science|AAAS]] Chemistry Section nominated, but then did not proceed with the nomination of Harran for [[American Association for the Advancement of Science|AAAS]] Fellow, after concerns about the Sangji case were raised by the [[American Chemical Society|ACS]] Committee on Chemical Safety.<ref>url=https://www.aaas.org/news/aaas-section-requests-permission-re-review-election-patrick-harran-fellow |access date=23 July 2021</ref>

==Research==
Harran's research is focused on the [[total synthesis]] of [[natural products]], design of novel chemical compounds to study [[protein–protein interaction]]s, and [[medicinal chemistry]].<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.chem.ucla.edu/harran/Research.html | title = Harran Research Group - Research Interests | publisher = University of California at Los Angeles | url-status = dead | archiveurl = https://web.archive.org/web/20150418233354/http://www.chem.ucla.edu/harran/Research.html | archivedate = 2015-04-18 }}</ref>

==Laboratory fire==
{{main|Sheri Sangji case}}
On December 29, 2008, a fire in Harran's UCLA laboratory fatally burned research assistant Sheri Sangji. Harran in 2011 was charged with four felony counts of willfully violating occupational safety standards in the case, carrying a maximum jail term of 4.5 years. It was the first time any American academic had been criminally charged for a laboratory accident. Representatives of Harran, and the university's Board of Regents who were also charged in the incident, disputed the charges.<ref name="Christensen 2014">{{citation|title=UCLA chemistry professor avoids prison time in fatal lab fire case|url=http://www.latimes.com/local/lanow/la-me-ln-ucla-professor-avoids-prison-fatal-lab-fire-20140620-story.html|newspaper=[[Los Angeles Times]]|first=Kim|last=Christensen|date=June 20, 2014}}.</ref><ref name="Christensen 2012">{{citation|title=Report faults professor, UCLA in death of lab assistant|newspaper=[[Los Angeles Times]]|first=Kim|last=Christensen|date=January 21, 2012|url=http://www.latimes.com/local/la-me-ucla-lab-20120121-story.html}}.</ref>

Harran and prosecutors in 2014 reached a deferred prosecution agreement in which Harran was ordered to pay $10,000 to a local burn center and do 800 hours of community service.<ref name="Christensen 2014" /><ref name="Benderly 2014">{{cite web|last1=Benderly|first1=Beryl|title=The Landmark Patrick Harran Case Ends Inconclusively|url=https://www.science.org/content/article/landmark-patrick-harran-case-ends-inconclusively|website=Taken for Granted|publisher=AAAS|accessdate=26 October 2014|date=2014-07-09}}</ref> Deputy District Attorney Craig W. Hum said that the penalty was similar to any sentence Harran would have received if convicted, while Sangji's family criticized it as "barely a slap on the wrist".<ref name="Benderly 2014"/> The charges were subsequently dropped in 2018, in accordance with the settlement terms.<ref>{{cite web|accessdate=2020-05-07|title=Charges dropped against UCLA chemistry professor Patrick Harran for death of Sheri Sangji after lab fire|url=https://cen.acs.org/safety/lab-safety/Charges-dropped-against-UCLA-chemistry/96/web/2018/09|website=Chemical & Engineering News}}</ref>
